clue.text: Hitchcock film from 29 26

indicators.note: 26 across reads 'organised', so the number stands for that word and tells us to put these letters into a new order

parts.note: 29 across, the limelight entry, supplies the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A film by Hitchcock is said to come from a pair of other clue answers.
explanation.walkthrough: In this puzzle '26' is shorthand for the word 'organised', which serves as an anagram signal: rearrange CENTRESTAGE (29 across) to get the film title. Secret Agent is a 1936 Hitchcock thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret Agent is the title of a 1936 thriller directed by Alfred Hitchcock.

clue.text: They're designed to cause shock waves

definitions.text: They're designed to cause shock waves

parts.words: They're designed to cause shock waves
parts.note: reads like a description of explosives or seismic devices, but a 'shock' is a mass of hair, so these are hairdressers or tongs that put waves into hair

explanation.surface: A description of weapons engineered to send out blast waves.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock of hair is a thick mass of it; people or tools that set waves into it are crimpers, a British slang word for hairdressers as well as for hair tongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimpers are hairdressers or curling tongs, which put waves into a head of hair.

clue.text: Number this number 26

indicators.note: 26 across reads 'organised', so the number stands for that word and asks for the letters to be put in a fresh order

parts.note: the clue is 3 down, so the number of this clue is three

explanation.surface: A puzzle about counting where the clue refers to its own number.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Number' is a numb-er, something that numbs: an anaesthetic. 'this number' is the clue's own number, 3, and '26' (organised) rearranges THREE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was used as an anaesthetic, a substance that makes a patient numb, so it is a numb-er.

clue.text: He won't believe suspect finally framed in a robbery

indicators.note: something framed sits inside a surround, so the letter is placed within the other pieces

parts.note: a heist is a robbery, especially a daring one

indicators.note: finally picks out the closing letter of the word suspect

explanation.surface: A suspect is set up for a robbery and protests that nobody will believe him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'framed' suggests a stitch-up, but here it means placed inside: the T at the end of 'suspect' goes into A HEIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist is a person who rejects belief in any god.

clue.text: Wrap up post very neatly, but only a couple

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the assembled letters are read from bottom to top, so the whole run is turned round

parts.note: a post is a pole, an upright stake

indicators.note: only a couple of letters of neatly survive, its opening pair, so the rest are dropped

explanation.surface: Advice to wrap a parcel for posting very neatly, but just two of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrap up' looks like the definition, but 'up' is the signal to read POLE + V + NE upwards. NE comes from 'neatly' keeping only its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop something is to enclose or cover it completely, as one would wrap it.

clue.text: Sing mostly about pilots mounting mock battle

indicators.note: about means the shortened word is placed around the pilots
mostly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to sing is criminal slang for informing, or talking to the police
the RAF, Britain's Royal Air Force, supplies pilots

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means the word climbs, so it is read backwards

parts.note: to rag someone is to tease or mock them

explanation.surface: A choir rehearses while airmen stage a pretend battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing' is criminal slang for inform, so it means talk. 'mock battle' is a false phrase: 'mock' belongs to the wordplay, and 'mounting' turns its synonym upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Trafalgar was the 1805 naval battle in which Nelson defeated the French and Spanish fleets.

clue.text: Criminal hiding by count

indicators.note: hiding means the given letters are kept out of sight, so they are removed from the longer word

parts.note: a baddy is a villain or criminal
taken as written

explanation.surface: A villain lurking near a nobleman with the title of count.
explanation.walkthrough: BADDY loses the scattered letters B and Y ('by'), leaving ADD. 'count' looks like a nobleman but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To add up is to count or total numbers.

clue.text: China almost stopping an ISP delivering explosive

indicators.note: stopping means the shortened word plugs a gap inside the other

parts.note: AOL, America Online, is an internet service provider

indicators.note: almost means the final letter of the word is left off

parts.note: china is Cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate = mate)

explanation.surface: A friend interrupts an internet provider's delivery of explosives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country: in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so a friend. 'an' and 'delivering' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Amatol is a high explosive made from TNT mixed with ammonium nitrate.

clue.text: Attractive woman sitting on chap, having left off robe

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so it comes first
having left off means one letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: doll is slang for an attractive woman
a man is a chap

explanation.surface: An attractive woman perched on a man's lap leaves behind her robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attractive woman sitting on chap' paints a lap scene; in a down entry, 'sitting on' simply means placed above. 'left' gives the dropped L.
explanation.definitionFit: A dolman is a long Turkish robe open at the front, or a hussar's jacket worn like a cape.

clue.text: Whicker in Hornsey, say? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means the final letter is left off

parts.note: Hornsey is a north London district with the postcode N8, read as N plus the word eight

explanation.surface: The broadcaster Alan Whicker visits a north London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Whicker was a British TV presenter, but a whicker is a horse's whinny. Hornsey, in north London, has the postcode N8: N + EIGHT, less its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A whicker is the soft whinnying sound a horse makes.

clue.text: Enjoy oneself as a part-eunuch might?

definitions.meaning: a man who has lost only one testicle could be said to keep one of them

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark on how a half-castrated man might enjoy himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to have a thoroughly good time; literally, a man missing one testicle still possesses a single one.

clue.text: Just one pawn to be captured by military

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: being captured by means going inside, so the letter is held within the longer word

parts.note: martial means relating to war or the military
P is the chess notation for a pawn

explanation.surface: A chess note: a single pawn is taken by the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' is an adjective here, meaning fair, not 'only'. P goes inside MARTIAL after I.
explanation.definitionFit: A just judge is fair and unbiased, treating all sides equally.

clue.text: Note short Roman nose

parts.note: A is a musical note

indicators.note: short means the last letter of the word is cut

explanation.surface: A remark about a Roman's short nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nose' is a noun meaning a wine's smell, not a facial feature. ROMAN cut short gives ROMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine's nose is its bouquet or smell, so the word means a characteristic scent.

clue.text: Cover chap without weapon

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the man's letters surround the weapon

parts.note: gent is short for gentleman, a chap
an arm is a weapon, as in firearms

explanation.surface: A man without a weapon seeks cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here it carries its old sense of 'outside', so the man surrounds the weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment is an item of clothing, something that covers the body.

clue.text: Rudimentary income run by 26

indicators.note: 26 across reads 'organised', standing for that word and asking for the letters to be arranged anew

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Income that comes in only at a basic, early level.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' stands for 'organised', the anagram signal: INCOME, R and BY are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Embryonic means at an early, undeveloped stage, just as rudimentary does.

clue.text: Servant's misfortune to be kicked out of sack

indicators.note: being kicked out of a word means those letters are removed from it

parts.note: to sack a town is to pillage it
an ill is a misfortune or trouble

explanation.surface: A servant has the bad luck to be fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sack' looks like dismissal, which fits a servant, but it means plunder: PILLAGE without ILL leaves PAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A page is a boy attendant or servant, as in a royal household.

clue.text: Nice 26 had a housing estate

indicators.note: housing means the two words hold the rearranged letters between them
26 across reads 'organised', standing for that word and asking for a new order of letters

explanation.surface: A pleasant housing estate in the French city of Nice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing estate' is a false phrase: 'housing' is the container signal, and '26' (organised) rearranges the French city's name before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacienda is a large landed estate or ranch in Spain or Latin America.

clue.text: Identify mine, catching a whiff

indicators.note: catching means the word holds the other letter inside it

parts.note: a dig is an excavation, as a mine is
to nose is to smell or sniff out, catching a whiff

explanation.surface: A miner identifies gas by catching a whiff of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' looks like a possessive but is a noun, an excavation; 'whiff' acts as a verb sense, to smell out.
explanation.definitionFit: To diagnose a problem is to identify its nature from the symptoms.

clue.text: Wader bird only half settled in islands

indicators.note: settled in means the piece is placed inside the other
only half means just the first half of the word bird is kept

explanation.surface: A wading bird has only half settled on some islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wader bird' looks like the definition, but 'bird' is the material: only its first half is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-legged wading bird with a down-curved bill.

clue.text: Registers guilt, initially stopping pride and envy?

indicators.note: stopping means the letter plugs a gap inside the word

parts.note: pride is one of the seven deadly sins

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of guilt

parts.note: envy is another of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to guilt about pride and envy.
explanation.walkthrough: Pride and envy are both among the seven deadly sins, giving SIN and SIN. G, from the start of 'guilt', plugs the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who registers at a hotel or office signs in on arrival.

clue.text: Worry about clergyman with one hell of a fast car?

indicators.note: about means the worry's letters go around the clergyman

parts.note: fear is worry or anxiety
RR stands for Right Reverend, a senior clergyman's title
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A vicar frets over a terrifyingly fast car.
explanation.walkthrough: RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's style. 'one hell of a' looks like a single phrase, but 'one' gives a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferrari is an Italian maker of very fast sports and racing cars.

clue.text: One who starts company's collapse

definitions.meaning: a person who sets up a firm or institution
to give way or sink, as a ship or building does

explanation.surface: A firm's start-up figure brings about its collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: A founder establishes an organisation; to founder is to fail or sink.

clue.text: Commercial about non- English fruit tree

indicators.note: about means the advert's letters surround the rest

parts.note: an ad is a commercial or advertisement

indicators.note: non- means the letter is taken away from the word that follows

parts.note: a lemon is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: An advert describes a fruit tree that is not from England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fruit tree' is a false phrase: 'fruit' is the material, and 'non- English' removes the abbreviation for English from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The almond is a tree of the rose family, grown for its edible nut.

clue.text: Rough stoned diamonds must be cut on the top

indicators.text: must be cut on the top
indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the start, so the letter is cut from the front

parts.note: stoned is slang for drugged
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Uncut stones that must be shaped by a jeweller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stoned diamonds' suggests gems, but 'stoned' means DRUGGED and 'diamonds' is D, removed from the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugged ground is rough, uneven and rocky.

clue.text: Rotten of you and me to block non-opening gambit

indicators.note: to block means the letters are put in the way, inside the other word
non-opening means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a ploy is a gambit or tactic
us means you and me

explanation.surface: Two players thwart a dirty opening move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gambit' brings chess openings to mind, but it just means a tactic; 'non-opening' removes its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lousy is informal for very bad or poor, so rotten in that sense.

clue.text: Tough girl almost lunges 26

indicators.note: 26 across reads 'organised', standing for that word and asking for these letters to be rearranged
almost means the final letter is left off the word

explanation.surface: A tough girl makes lunges during an exercise class.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' stands for 'organised', the anagram signal: GIRL and LUNGE (from 'lunges' minus its last letter) are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A gruelling task is tough and exhausting.

clue.text: Thugs pulling up top of tiny flower

indicators.note: pulling up in a down clue moves a letter higher, nearer the start

parts.note: louts are thugs or hooligans

explanation.surface: Thugs uproot a tiny flower.
explanation.walkthrough: The T is the 'top of tiny': it is raised one place in LOUTS, giving LOTUS.
explanation.definitionFit: The lotus is a water lily, a flowering aquatic plant.

clue.text: Ran right into 17 26

indicators.note: into means the letter is placed inside the other word
the clue's own number is used, as elsewhere in the puzzle, as an instruction to rearrange letters

parts.note: 17 down, meaning identify, supplies letters

explanation.surface: Someone ran right into a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue uses its own entry as the anagram signal, which seems odd until the solver has cracked other cross-references. 'Ran' means managed, as one would arrange an event.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who ran an event managed it, and to manage something is to arrange or coordinate it.

clue.text: Dance as Brown takes leave

parts.note: tan is a brown colour
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: A sunburnt person heads off to a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is a link: TAN is followed by GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a Latin American ballroom dance.

clue.text: Pop Idol had idiots taking second places

indicators.note: taking second places picks the second letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A TV talent show had some fools coming second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop Idol' was a British TV talent show, but 'Pop' is the definition and 'Idol' is one of the words read.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is an informal word for a father.

clue.text: 1 Across 26 receiving attention

indicators.note: 26 across reads 'organised', standing for that word and asking for these letters to be rearranged

parts.note: 1 across, the Hitchcock film, supplies the letters

explanation.surface: A film title placed in the limelight.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' stands for 'organised', the anagram signal: SECRETAGENT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the centre of the stage is to be in the spotlight, the focus of attention.
